Title: Document 3b
Content: From the inception of the woman suffrage movement through the ratification of the `text(Nineteenth)` Amendment in `1920`, there were women and men who vigorously opposed it. Antisuffrage individuals and groups obstructed the enfranchisement of women for a multitude of reasons. Early antisuffragists of the late `text(1860s)` and `text(1870s)` were primarily concerned that the ballot would disrupt women’s domestic and maternal roles and create disharmony in the family. Horace Greeley, `text(one)` of the most influential antisuffragists of this era, asserted that the vast majority of women had no interest in voting or in politics. In `1871`, conservative domestic authority Catharine Beecher and the wives of General William Sherman and Admiral John Dahlgren delivered to Congress a petition containing `text(1,000)` women’s signatures pleading with Congress to desist [refrain] from enacting a law enfranchising women. Beecher, in her book Woman Suffrage and Woman’s Profession, proclaimed that if women were given the vote, most would consider it an overwhelming burden that would cause them to shortchange their domestic duties. . . .
